parts.title: Jupiter's brightest auroras are powered by Alfvén waves that start right where the light is made
parts.abstract:
Jupiter has the brightest auroras in the solar system. Auroras are the glowing lights that form when fast-moving electrons crash into a planet's upper atmosphere. On Jupiter, these electrons are extremely energetic, and their numbers change a great deal from moment to moment.

In this paper, we build a complete set of equations that accurately describes the two main ways these electrons are sped up, which we call the two "modes" of auroral acceleration. We show that which of the two modes appears depends on particular length scales in the plasma, the hot, electrically charged gas that fills the space around the planet. The key comparison is between the width of the region where the electrons are sped up, measured across the magnetic field lines, and the electron inertial length. The electron inertial length is a tiny distance that sets how far electrons can move before they can no longer simply follow the electric field.

Scientists have long accepted that the Alfvén waves responsible for speeding up these electrons start far away, near Jupiter's equator. Alfvén waves are ripples in a magnetic field that travel along it. We show that these waves can also be made right there, close to Jupiter's surface. From this understanding, we find that Alfvén waves made at these low altitudes can directly speed up the most intense auroral electrons at Jupiter.

These findings show that the low-altitude region where electrons are sped up can itself become a source of Alfvén waves, rather than only a place where wave energy is used up. This changes the standard picture of how energy moves through the magnetosphere, the region of space shaped by a planet's magnetic field, on planets with strong magnetic fields.
parts.introduction_first:
Before NASA's Juno spacecraft arrived, it was the first satellite to orbit Jupiter and pass over its poles. Before Juno, scientists explained the brightness and position of Jupiter's main auroral oval, the ring of glowing light around each pole, with a model of a steady, unchanging system. In this model, the magnetosphere (the region of space shaped by the planet's magnetic field) and the ionosphere (the electrically charged upper layer of the atmosphere) are linked.

In the middle of the magnetosphere, the plasma, the hot charged gas, stops being carried around by the planet's magnetic field. This creates electric currents. These currents limit how much the plasma can lag behind the planet's rotation, by passing angular momentum (the "spin" of the system) from the polar ionosphere to the plasma. Electrons flow along the magnetic field lines as the carriers of this current and crash into the polar ionosphere, which makes the aurora glow.

This model was first developed for Earth's aurora (1). It links the electric current flowing along the magnetic field lines to the voltage drop along them, and scientists applied that link to Jupiter [e.g., (2, 3)]. It was therefore natural to expect that the electrons above Jupiter that power the aurora would all have about the same energy, a "monoenergetic" distribution. In that picture, each electron would gain one fixed amount of energy, qφ||, as it falls through the voltage drop and is sped up downward into Jupiter's ionosphere. Here q is the electron's charge and φ|| is the voltage drop along the magnetic field line.
parts.introduction_rest:
However, Juno's early observations above the auroral zones showed something different. Most of the electrons there did not all have about the same energy. Instead, their energies were spread out over a wide range, which we call a "broadband" distribution. This happened along the magnetic field lines at low altitudes, close to the planet (4, 5). Later studies that counted these electrons found that the vast majority of electron populations along the field lines are broadband, not peaked at one energy (6). This raised a question: what could explain these wide energy spreads?

Two possible explanations were put forward. The first was inertial Alfvén waves. These are Alfvén waves that interact with electrons at the small scales where the electric field along the magnetic field lines becomes large (7–12). The second was whistler-mode waves, a different kind of wave that travels along magnetic field lines. These waves would speed up electrons through a random, step-by-step process (13–16).

A recent discovery tips the balance toward Alfvén waves (17). The auroral ionosphere is significantly and persistently depleted, meaning it holds far fewer electrons than usual. Whistler-mode waves cannot travel above the electron plasma frequency, a natural frequency set by how many electrons there are. In a medium with so few electrons, whistler-mode waves would therefore be held back. An inertial Alfvén wave, on the other hand, is better able to build up an electric field along the magnetic field lines when there are few electrons.

To see why, we need to consider the motion of individual electrons. At these low altitudes, the electrons' inertia, their tendency to resist being pushed, becomes important. Electrons then take a little time to respond. They can no longer instantly cancel out any electric field along the magnetic field lines. The usual simplified description of a plasma, called ideal magnetohydrodynamics, no longer holds. In this "inertial limit", the Alfvén wave's dispersion relation, the rule that links a wave's frequency to its wavelength, becomes

(ωk‖cA)2=1+k⊥2ρi21+k⊥2λe2≈11+k⊥2λe2(1)

Here ω is the angular frequency, which tells how fast the wave oscillates. k‖ and k⊥ are the wave numbers along and across the magnetic field lines, which tell how tightly the wave is packed in space. cA is the Alfvén speed, cA = VA/(1 + VA2/c2)1/2, where VA is the usual Alfvén speed and c is the speed of light. This speed is modified by the displacement current, the electric current that appears when the electric field changes over time. λe is the electron inertial length, and ρi is the ion gyroradius, the radius of the circle an ion makes as it spirals around a magnetic field line.

The term k⊥2ρi2 in Eq. 1 can be ignored when β < me/mp. Here β is the ratio of the thermal pressure, the pressure from the random motion of particles, to the magnetic pressure, and me/mp is the ratio of the electron's mass to the proton's mass. For Jupiter, β is about 10−8, so this condition is well satisfied in its low-altitude auroral zones.

Jupiter's main auroral oval is fed by two regions of current. Zone I carries current upward, and Zone II carries current downward (18, 19). One unexpected feature at Jupiter is that bright auroral light is seen in the downward current region, Zone II. This region carries large downward flows of electrons, even though the current flows the other way.

Whether Alfvén waves speed up electrons at Jupiter, and how important this is, is still largely assumed, although there are strong theoretical arguments for it. Scientists have seen low-frequency (0.2 to 5 Hz) ripples in the magnetic field that point across the field lines and have been interpreted as Alfvén waves. These ripples clearly line up with the diffuse aurora, the faint, spread-out glow, which lies closer to the equator than Zones I and II. Similar ripples have also been reported very high up, more than 10 times Jupiter's radius above the planet (20). At those heights, it is unclear which magnetic field lines connect to the main auroral zones.

Several ideas have been offered to explain why these ripples are missing above the main auroral zones. The ripples might be used up quickly (19). The instruments might not be sensitive enough (21). Or the inertial Alfvén wave might become more and more electric in nature, so that it shows up only weakly in the magnetic field.

There is also a question of where the waves come from. Alfvén waves at Jupiter's high latitudes are thought to come only from the equatorial plasma sheet, the region of plasma near the equator. This is likely because of turbulence stirred up by plasma flowing outward (7), and/or because of instabilities set off by large temperature anisotropies, where the plasma is much hotter in one direction than in another (22). This is different from the Alfvén waves along the flux tube that links Io, one of Jupiter's moons, to the planet. Those waves have a known source: they begin as distortions of the magnetic field with a wavelength about as long as Io's extended diameter (23–25).

The highest frequency an Alfvén wave can reach is the proton cyclotron frequency, the rate at which protons spiral around the magnetic field. At 30 times Jupiter's radius near the equator, this is about 1 Hz. Juno's plasma wave instrument can measure the electric field (E) and the magnetic field (B) at the same time only from 50 Hz upward. So, using Juno's measurements, we cannot say for certain that the Alfvén-like ripples at the high latitudes come from the equator.

By contrast, Alfvén waves made at low altitudes can travel upward at frequencies up to about a kilohertz, the proton cyclotron frequency in the polar region. This is well within the range of Juno's plasma wave instrument. However, Juno measures at only one point at a time. Without measurements at several points, we cannot study how E and B change with the wave number k, which is needed to tell the two kinds of waves apart. That said, proton cyclotron waves, which are waves that travel at different speeds for different wavelengths, are often measured above Jupiter's auroral zones. These are likely the high-frequency part of Alfvén waves made at low altitudes (19, 26, 27), though this evidence should be treated as circumstantial rather than direct.
parts.methods:
## Materials and methods

### How much energy the electrons carry

We work out the energy flux, which is the total energy carried by electrons each second, for electrons with energies from 30 to 1000 keV. (A keV, or kiloelectronvolt, is a unit of energy.) We count only electrons that travel downward inside the "loss cone". This is a narrow range of directions, like a funnel, in which electrons can reach the planet's upper atmosphere and crash into it. The energy flux is

Energy flux = π ∫ from Emin to Emax of I · E dE (5)

Here I is the particle intensity, the number of electrons arriving each second on each square centimetre, from each direction in the sky, for each keV of energy (cm−2 s−1 sr−1 keV−1). E is the electron's energy (keV). The symbol π stands for the size of the loss cone, weighted by the area it covers when seen from above.

We estimate how wide the loss cone is by treating Jupiter's magnetic field as a simple dipole, the same shape as a bar magnet. In that case the width is arcsin(1/R3)1/2, where R is the distance from Jupiter's centre, measured in Jovian radii (the radius of Jupiter).

### Electric current flowing along the magnetic field lines

We estimate how strong the electric current flowing along the magnetic field lines is, and whether it flows upward or downward. To do this, we use Ampère's law, following the method in (49). Ampère's law says that a changing magnetic field is linked to the electric current that makes it.

First, we find how much the magnetic field has been disturbed, which we call the magnetic field perturbation:

δB = BMAG − BJRM33 (50)

BMAG is the magnetic field measured by Juno's MAG instrument, recorded once every second. BJRM33 is the magnetic field predicted by a computer model. We average the perturbation over Juno's 30-second spin period, the time it takes the spacecraft to turn once around its axis. This removes leftover effects of the spacecraft's own spinning.

The model magnetic field comes from two models of the magnetic field, one for the field inside Jupiter and one for the field outside it. Both are treated as unchanging over time. The internal model, JRM33, includes the field up to order and degree 13, which means it captures the field's shape in fine detail. The external model is Con2020 (51, 52). We use both through the JupiterMag Python wrapper (53), a software tool that runs these models.

We apply Ampère's law in a set of directions centred on the spacecraft. These directions follow a right-hand rule, the same one used for screw threads. The z direction, zˆ, points along the local magnetic field, bˆ. The y direction, yˆ, points along the spacecraft's speed across the magnetic field, v⊥. The x direction, xˆ, points along v×bˆ, which is the direction you get by turning the speed vector 90 degrees toward the magnetic field.

The spacecraft travels along a single line, so it can only measure one direction. This limits how we can calculate the "curl" in Ampère's law, a measure of how much the magnetic field twists around a point. As a result, only one of the two parts of the z component of the curl can be measured. Other researchers have included both parts by splitting the spacecraft's path into two speed components (17). However, this risks making the current look stronger than it really is, and making that extra strength uneven along the path. For these reasons, we calculate the current density flowing along the field lines, j‖, as

j‖ = −(1/μ0) · (ΔδBv×bˆ / xv⊥) = −(1/μ0) · (v⊥ / Δt) · (ΔδBv×bˆ / Δt) (6)

Here μ0 is the permeability of free space, a fixed number that describes how magnetic fields behave in empty space. ΔδBv×bˆ is the change in the magnetic field perturbation in the v×bˆ direction. v⊥ is the size of the spacecraft's speed across the magnetic field. xv⊥ is the spacecraft's position in the v⊥ direction, and t is time.

A single spacecraft has a built-in limit. It cannot tell apart changes that happen over time from changes that happen from place to place. So a change in the magnetic field cannot be traced to electric currents in only one way. Our calculation rests on one key assumption: the magnetic field changes mainly from place to place. This is reasonable, because we see the same disturbances again and again over the auroral zones, so they depend mostly on latitude.

With this assumption, we use the second form of the equation to estimate how the field changes from place to place from how it changes over time. We should also note that this method may give current values that are too low. That is because we assume the spacecraft crosses a current sheet at a right angle, and that the sheet is infinitely large. A current sheet is a thin layer where electric current flows. When the spacecraft crosses the sheet at a slant, the v×bˆ part of the magnetic field does not pick up the full disturbance the sheet creates.

### The equation that links waves to the plasma

We use the approach set out by Lysak and Lotko (54, 55). It describes how waves travel through the plasma. The equation we solve is called the dispersion relation. It links a wave's frequency, ω, to its wavelength, k, and tells us how the wave behaves.

We look at waves with a frequency below the ion (proton) cyclotron frequency, Ωci. This is the rate at which protons circle around the magnetic field lines. We also look at waves whose wavelength across the magnetic field is short, so that k⟂VA/Ωci ≫ 1. Here VA is the Alfvén speed, the speed at which Alfvén waves travel. Under these conditions, the fast MHD mode is cut off. This is a fast wave that travels along the magnetic field lines.

The response across the magnetic field lines comes mainly from the ions, the positively charged particles. The response along the field lines comes mainly from the electrons. The dispersion relation can be written as

n‖2 = S(1 − n⊥2P) (7)

S = 1 + c2VA2G(μi, ω/Ωci) (8)

P = 1 + Γ0(μe)k‖2λD2(1 + ξZ(ξ)) (9)

Here ξ = ω/k||ae, μi,e = k⟂2ρi,e2, ae = (2Te/me)½, λD = (ε0Te/ne2)½, and ρi = (miTi)½/eB. In these symbols, c is the speed of light, VA is the Alfvén speed, and Te and Ti are the electron and ion temperatures. The symbol λD is the Debye length, the distance over which electric charges in the plasma shield each other. The symbol ρi is the ion gyroradius, the size of the circle an ion makes as it circles the magnetic field.

G = 1 − Γ0(μi)μi + 2Γ1(μi)μiω2/Ωci21 − ω2/Ωci2 (10)

Here Γn(x) = e–xIn(x) is related to the modified Bessel function, a standard mathematical function. Z(ξ) is the plasma dispersion function, another standard function that describes how the plasma responds to waves. We solve the dispersion relation in this form:

(ωk‖c)2 = 11 + c2VA2G + k⊥2λD2k‖2λD2 + Γ0(μe)[1 + ξZ(ξ)] (11)

We find the roots of this equation using Muller's method, a step-by-step way of finding where a curve crosses zero. The roots are complex numbers, which have a real part and an imaginary part. The real part is the wave's frequency. The imaginary part is the growth rate, which tells us how quickly the wave grows or fades.

We model the electron beam as a drifting Maxwellian. This means the electrons in the beam have a spread of speeds, following the familiar bell-shaped curve, and the whole group moves together. The beam's density is 1% of the plasma density. The results depend only weakly on how dense the beam is. What mainly controls how the waves behave is the state of the plasma, namely its temperature, density and magnetic field, along with the beam's energy.
parts.results:
## Results

Figure 1 shows pictures of how brightly two of the events in this case study glowed in ultraviolet light. We made these pictures from images taken by Juno's Ultraviolet Spectrograph instrument (28) during two of its low-altitude passes over the aurora: the fourth pass over the southern pole (PJ4S) and the seventh pass over the northern pole (PJ7N). On top of the pictures we drew Juno's path, traced from the planet's magnetic field, with one point every minute.

Figure 2 shows what Juno's other instruments recorded during these same passes. Panels A and B show the electron energy flux, which is how much energy the electrons carry, for electrons with energies from 30 to 1000 keV. These electrons travel downward into the "loss cone". The loss cone is the narrow range of directions in which electrons can travel straight down along the magnetic field lines and crash into the atmosphere.

Panels C and D show the electric current flowing along the magnetic field lines, which we call the field-aligned current density, j||. We worked it out from the magnetometer, Juno's instrument for measuring the magnetic field (29). It records small changes in the magnetic field, which we averaged over 30 seconds and subtracted the background. This record is reliable for telling when Juno crossed the main aurora. It is especially good at separating the upward current region (Zone I) from the downward current region (Zone II) (see Materials and Methods).

Panels E and F show the electron number density, ne, which is how many electrons there are in each cubic centimetre. They also show the electron inertial length, λe. We worked both out from the particle measurements and from the cutoffs of plasma waves. Outside the main aurora, toward the equator, most of these points come from the Jovian Auroral Distributions Experiment, or JADE (30, 31). Closer to the pole, including inside the main aurora, the points come from the lowest frequency of a type of radio emission called ordinary-mode emission, measured by the Waves instrument (17, 32–34).

Where auroral electrons are being sped up, the plasma is strongly magnetized. This means the electrons circle the magnetic field lines far more often than they bounce off the waves in the plasma. In symbols, fpe ≪ fce, where fpe is the electron plasma frequency and fce is the electron cyclotron frequency. The plasma is also very thin there. The electron density is of order 10−2 cm−3, and the electron inertial length is of order 10 km.

Panels G and H, and I and J, show the energy and pitch angle of electrons with 30 to 1000 keV, measured by the Jupiter Energetic-particle Detector Instrument, or JEDI (35). The pitch angle is the angle between an electron's direction of travel and the magnetic field line. We calculated the loss cone angles and drew them on top of these pitch angle measurements. We only used the JEDI data from the stretches of time when Juno crossed the main auroral zones.

**Fig. 1. Ultraviolet pictures of Jupiter's aurora.**

Ultraviolet brightness pictures taken by the Ultraviolet Spectrograph (UVS) (28, 56, 57) for (A) PJ4S and (B) PJ7N, shown as flat maps. On top are Juno's path, traced from the magnetic field, in white, and the statistical main auroral oval in orange (58). A cross marks the magnetic pole. White rings highlight the main auroral crossings we studied. Yellow lines point toward the Sun. The time between when the in-situ measurements were taken and when the UV pictures were taken is not constant, so this figure is shown only for context.

**Fig. 2. Data from several instruments during Juno's fourth (southern) and seventh (northern) low-altitude auroral passes.**

(A and B) Electron energy flux in the downward loss cone, measured by JEDI for energies from 30 to 1000 keV. (C and D) Field-aligned current densities, worked out from 30-second averages of changes in the magnetic field measured by the magnetometer. (E and F) Electron number densities, worked out from plasma wave cutoffs measured by the Waves instrument (black) and from the JADE measurements of the electron distribution (gray). (G and H) Energy-time spectrograms of energetic electrons in the loss cone measured by JEDI. (I and J) Pitch-angle time spectrograms of energetic electrons, with the loss cone angles drawn as dashed white lines. BB, broadband; Mono, monoenergetic.

The PJ4S event shows electron distributions that are typical for Jupiter's auroral zones. It is a typical example of what is seen there. The currents are powered by both monoenergetic and broadband acceleration. In broadband acceleration, electrons gain a wide range of energies. This broadband process makes up most of the electron distributions that are seen (6).

The monoenergetic distributions are thought to come from electrostatic acceleration. This means the electrons are sped up by an electric field rather than by a magnetic one. The field can come from a double layer, a thin region where the electric field is very strong. It can also come from small, local electric fields along the field lines, which are set up by field line resonances. These monoenergetic electrons are often seen together with protons that are sped up in the opposite direction, both along the field lines.

In energy-time plots, these monoenergetic electrons form "inverted-V" shapes. We interpret these shapes as changes from place to place across a voltage structure that stays almost the same over time. The top of the V marks the point where electrons fall through the largest voltage drop. This is strikingly similar to what is seen above Earth's auroral oval, although the voltages at Jupiter are much higher (36, 37). These structures are generally thought to be part of a large electric current circuit. A "generator" drives the current, and a "load" uses it up (38, 39). At Jupiter, the electric currents are needed to balance the curl of the magnetic field, ∇ × B, which is set by the plasma flowing through the magnetosphere.

The broadband distributions are different. They are linked to electrons that travel along the field lines in both directions, and sometimes in only one. There is no sign that ions are being sped up along the field lines at the same time. Both kinds of distribution have been studied a great deal at Jupiter. It has been shown that both seem to have a similar link between energy flux and characteristic energy, the typical energy of the electrons. Because of this, either one can broadly explain the UV brightness and the ratio of UV colours that are seen (40).

This brings us back to the question, in the words of Mauk et al. (41): Why is either process favored at any one time? Figure 2 shows that both distributions can appear in the same current region, with the same current direction and the same current strength. Even so, the local plasma conditions change a great deal from place to place. Between the first broadband distribution, at 13:38:35, and the inverted-V, at 13:38:49, the electron density falls steeply from 0.20 to 0.01 cm−3, while the current stays fairly steady. Between the inverted-V and the second distribution, at 13:39:08, the density stays steady, but the current flips direction. This makes it hard to study which distribution is preferred.

PJ7N is a rare event in which the two acceleration processes seem to work together, and their distributions are clearly separate, as Fig. 2H shows. Nothing like this has been seen before in Earth's auroral regions (18, 42, 43). That makes the event a natural choice for studying how the broadband distributions at Jupiter get started.

Figure 2J shows that the electrons are mostly sped up in the downward loss cone. The downward energy flux is highest during the broadband interval. The upward loss cone is mostly empty, although there is a group of electrons just outside it, mostly during the broadband interval. The whole event happens inside an upward field-aligned current whose strength stays almost steady.

In this region the density measurements are patchy, with a gap ranging from 0.02 to 0.12 cm−3 over 25 s. The inverted-V covers the widest region where the electrons are sped up. We estimated the density across it by filling in the gaps between measurements on a log-linear scale, a scale that is even in steps of ten. This gives a density between 0.05 and 0.10 cm−3, with a value of 0.07 cm−3 during the broadband interval. The magnetic field is measured at 170 μT.

Mauk et al. (41) asked one question in particular. Did the broadband distribution happen at the same time as the inverted-V, meaning the double layer stayed in place the whole time? Or did the system switch from one mode to the other? We looked at the pitch angles of the ions during this event. Where the inverted-V was seen, the ions were being sped up upward by an electric field. This supports the idea that a double layer with a converging electric field was present.

Where the broadband acceleration was seen, however, the upward ions seemed to be held back. Instead, they formed a cone-shaped spread of pitch angles. From this, we concluded that the broadband process was replacing the monoenergetic process, rather than existing alongside it (see fig. S1). The broadband acceleration also carried the strongest electron energy fluxes, about 3000 mW/m2 (Fig. 2B). The broadband distribution appeared where the top of the inverted-V would have been, the point of highest energy. This suggests that the system became unstable once the energy passed a threshold of 300 keV.

### Inertial Alfvén wave theory

We start with some calculations based on cold plasma theory. In this theory, the particles are treated as if they had no temperature, so they all move at the same speed. We also use Landau resonance, where ω/k|| = vbeam. Here ω is the wave's frequency, k|| is the wave number along the field line, and vbeam is the speed of the electron beam. In words, the wave travels along the field line at the same speed as the beam.

Using Eq. 1, we put vbeam = 0.77c on the left-hand side, as shown in Fig. 3C. This speed matches an energy of 300 keV once the effects of relativity are included. We also put cA = 0.9998c, where cA is the Alfvén speed. This gives k⟂λe = 0.82. Here k⟂ is the wave number across the field lines, and λe is the electron inertial length. A density of 0.07 cm−3 gives λe = 20 km. This in turn gives k⟂ = 0.0415 km−1, or a width across the field lines of 2π/k⟂ = 151 km.

**Fig. 3. Normalized growth rates for the PJ7N event.**

Calculated for beam energy against k⟂λe for (A) Te = 15 keV and (B) 20 keV. (C) Phase speed against k⟂λe, from the inertial Alfvén wave dispersion relation in Eq. 1. The phase speed that matches a beam speed of 0.77c, or 300 keV, is marked. (D) Beam energy against normalized growth rates, with a 300-keV beam energy marked. The red region is unstable, where the growth rate is positive.

Next, we compare this with the distance Juno travelled across the broadband region. This gives an estimate of the width across the field lines. We found it by multiplying Juno's speed across the field lines by the time it spent in the region. The result is a similar value, 0.05 km−1, or 120 km. This matches k⟂λe = 1. By contrast, the inverted-V matches k⟂λe = 0.2.

We now look at how the electric and magnetic fields of an inertial Alfvén wave are related. The parallel electric field and the ratio of the electric to the magnetic field are given by

E‖=k‖k⊥λe21+k⊥2λe2E⊥(2)

E⊥B⊥=cA(1+k⊥2λe2)1/2(3)

Here E‖ is the electric field along the field lines, E⊥ is the electric field across them, and B⊥ is the magnetic field across them. The electron inertial length is λe = c/ωpe. Here c is the speed of light, and ωpe = (nee2/ε0me)1/2 is the electron plasma frequency. It is easy to see that a low electron density, ne, helps a parallel electric field to build up. That, in turn, helps to speed up electrons along the field lines.

We estimate the voltage delivered by an inertial Alfvén wave by combining Eqs. 2 and 3 to get

Δφ‖=B⊥cAλek⊥λe(1+k⊥2λe2)1/2(4)

Using the known quantities and the measured B⟂ = about 100 nT, we get a largest voltage drop of Δφ = 380 kV. This fully fits the high energies seen in the broadband electrons. Together, these results strongly suggest that the inertial Alfvén wave is made right there, close to the surface, by monoenergetic electron beams that are sped up to more than 300 keV.

The waves travel at close to the speed of light, cA ∼ c. So they can only interact with slower electrons in a nonresonant way (44). In other words, the electrons do not keep in step with the wave. The plasma is not the same everywhere, as in the auroral flux tube, the column of plasma above the aurora. So, in each electron's own frame of reference, it feels an electric field along the field lines at that moment. The electron is sped up or slowed down along the magnetic field during part of the wave's cycle, before the wave moves on. This would show up as a distribution that covers a wide range of energies and travels in both directions, as is often seen in Jupiter's auroral zones.

### Beam-plasma instability

To test this idea further, we go beyond cold plasma theory and take the particles' temperature into account. We want to find out whether the measured k⟂λe and beam speed can lead to positive growth rates, which means instability. A growth rate tells how fast a small disturbance grows. A positive growth rate means the disturbance grows, so the beam can drive the wave.

Figure 3 (A and B) shows the normalized growth rates from a kinetic dispersion solver (see Materials and Methods). This is a computer program that solves the equations for how waves grow in a plasma that has a temperature. We recreated most of the plasma conditions in Fig. 2B. Using the estimated density and the measured magnetic field strength, we get ωpe/Ωci = 0.9. Here Ωci is the ion (H+) cyclotron frequency, the rate at which ions circle the magnetic field lines.

Above the main aurora, the electron temperature, Te, cannot be measured because the signal is too weak compared with the noise. It was measured up to the edge of the main aurora toward the equator, and it was found to rise toward the pole, reaching 13 keV at 1:15:55 (31). We treat this value as a lower limit, because Juno was farther toward the pole before that time. We solved for Te = 15 keV (Fig. 3A) and 20 keV (Fig. 3B). We added an electron beam to the background electrons. We modelled the beam as a drifting Maxwellian, a spread of speeds that is most common near the beam's speed.

The results show that instability happens only within a certain range. On one side is k⟂λe ∼ 1. On the other side is a lowest beam energy that depends on Te and rises as Te rises. Figure 3D looks at this more closely. It plots beam energies from 50 to 500 keV against the normalized growth rates. For comparison, we marked the 300 keV threshold seen in Fig. 2H.

We looked at four cases: Te = 15 and 20 keV, each with k⟂λe = 0.8 and 1. Overall, the best case is Te = 15 keV with k⟂λe = 0.8. In this case, the growth rates become positive as soon as the beam reaches the lowest energy threshold. The other three cases are also fairly close, and they broadly fit our estimates of Te and k⟂λe from Juno's measurements.

A similar event happened during the PJ10N auroral pass (41). However, the densities and field-aligned currents were not measured well enough for a similarly careful study. One sign of PJ4S, at 13:39:08, is unclear. The broadband distribution might look as if it appeared at the same time as the top of a narrow inverted-V. We cannot confirm that the inverted-V was really there, because the data are not detailed enough, and the ion data give no extra clues.

That said, if this was indeed an inverted-V, we can show that it would be unstable at its top, where the energy is above 100 keV in this event. During PJ4S, Te was found to be roughly half of PJ7N's. It also rose toward the pole, reaching 7.5 keV at the edge of Zone I toward the equator. Figure 3 (A and B) makes it clear that the lowest beam energy needed for instability goes down as Te goes down.

We calculated growth rates (fig. S2) for Te = 10 keV and k⟂λe = 1.5. In this case, the beam needs an energy of about 100 keV before the growth rate becomes positive. This would also explain the clean inverted-V at 13:38:49, whose peak energy is 100 keV. This voltage structure stretches over a much wider region, with k⟂λe = 0.5, and has a matching beam energy threshold of about 500 keV. So this voltage structure stays stable.

## Discussion

We combined measurements from several instruments, theory and computer models. Accurate measurements of how many electrons are packed into each bit of space made this possible. Together, they confirm that a type of Alfvén wave called an inertial Alfvén wave can be responsible for the broad, wide-ranging electron energy patterns that produce Jupiter's most intense auroras.

Earlier work treated ripples in the magnetic field that point across the field lines as Alfvén waves (45). Those waves were found to lie closer to the equator than the main aurora (19, 21). Scientists have long agreed that Alfvén waves play an important part in speeding up auroral electrons. But the usual idea was that these waves start in the middle of the magnetosphere, near the equator, and travel down to the low altitudes where the aurora forms. This may be true, but no one has yet seen it confirmed by observations.

We show that a beam instability at low altitudes can make Alfvén waves right there. A beam instability happens when a fast stream of electrons, called a beam, pushes against the plasma around it and sets it shaking. We also show that the broad energy patterns appear over a region where k⟂λe ≳ 1. Here k⟂ is the size of the wave's ripple across the magnetic field lines, and λe is the electron inertial length. This is the scale at which an inertial Alfvén wave can build up an electric field along the magnetic field lines. The monoenergetic patterns, and the inverted-V patterns, are linked to k⟂λe ≪ 1, meaning the ripples are much smaller than the electron inertial length.

Many things affect the physics here: the magnetic field, how strong the current is, how many electrons there are, how hot the electrons are, and how energetic the beam is. So we focused on one event, called PJ7N. In this event, monoenergetic and broad patterns appeared side by side, and the measurements were of the highest quality. Mauk and colleagues (41) first drew attention to this "bimodal" event, meaning one with two different patterns. They guessed that the instability might have started because the current became too high. Figure 2 (C and D) shows that this is not necessarily the case.

Finally, we turn to a question raised by Mauk and colleagues (41): why does the system pick one way of speeding up electrons (monoenergetic or broad) over the other at any given time or place? We conclude that the two are not independent. Instead, monoenergetic acceleration can be a necessary first step before broad acceleration can happen. Figure 4 is a drawing that sums up how we see this.

To understand why, it helps to know about a double layer. A double layer is a thin region where the voltage drops sharply along the magnetic field lines. It is well understood in a magnetized plasma where particles rarely bump into each other. In such a plasma, the electrons that are available cannot smoothly supply the current that is needed (1). In Jupiter's magnetosphere, the need for this current comes from plasma near the equator that lags behind the planet's rotation (46). It can also come from sudden, step-like changes in how plasma is carried along the magnetic field lines, which upset the balance of forces between the magnetosphere and the ionosphere (7). A double layer, and/or large-scale field line resonances (standing wave patterns along the whole length of a magnetic field line), can keep up the monoenergetic voltage drop. Together they create an electric field along the field lines in a small region (47, 48).

Fig. 4.

A drawing of the PJ7N auroral acceleration event.

The drawing links the electron energy pattern we observed to what is happening in space. The inverted-V pattern is linked to a nearly steady voltage structure (dashed lines). Its electric field points along the magnetic field lines and squeezes together, so it speeds electrons downward. The voltage drop grows larger toward the center, or apex, of the structure. When the electrons are sped up past a certain energy, an instability is triggered. This produces an inertial Alfvén wave through Landau resonance, a process in which electrons moving at the wave's speed ride along with it and give it energy. The wave travels along the magnetic field at close to the speed of light. Electrons that do not ride along with the wave still interact with it, and this produces a broad pattern of electrons moving in both directions. Jupiter image credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech/SwRI/MSSS.

Whether the monoenergetic beams of electrons traveling along the field lines set off an instability depends on several things in the low-altitude auroral zones. The most important are the electron temperature, which sets the lowest beam energy needed, and the electron density, which sets the electron inertial length. Once both conditions are met, inertial Alfvén waves made right there speed up electrons without riding along with the wave, and this sends the most energy in electrons to the highest levels.

If we see only an inverted-V pattern, the conditions for the instability have not been met. When these patterns are fully formed, as in Fig. 2G, their highest electron energies are only about 100 keV (keV, or kilo-electronvolts, is a unit of energy). This suggests that the beam has probably not reached the energy it needs. These patterns also stretch over a longer distance, or k⟂λe ≪ 1. In our chart of beam energy against k⟂λe, they are the regions where the instability does not grow.

A broad pattern on its own, on the other hand, could come from two possible sources. The first is that the conditions have been met. This is often seen over shorter distances, or k⟂λe ≳ 1. In that case, the beam that is already there probably comes from a double layer at an altitude away from the spacecraft. Double layers can move along the auroral magnetic field lines over a range of altitudes, but their electric fields along the field lines are very tightly confined. So we only see them when Juno crosses the auroral zones at the altitude where the double layer happens to be at that moment. The second possibility is that the electrons are sped up by dispersive Alfvén waves, which are Alfvén waves that spread out and change shape as they travel. These would come from the equatorial plasma sheet, the layer of plasma near the equator. This idea still needs to be confirmed by observations at Jupiter.

In this study, we built a framework that explains why auroral electrons at Jupiter show two different energy patterns. We showed that which pattern appears is controlled at its root by particular length scales in the plasma. The key is how the width of the region where electrons are sped up, measured across the magnetic field lines, compares with the electron inertial length. Our results also show that inertial Alfvén waves can be made right inside the low-altitude region where electrons are sped up. This is different from the usual picture, in which auroral Alfvén waves start only in distant regions near the equator. We find that these waves made at low altitudes can directly speed up electrons to the highest energy levels ever seen in the aurora. This links processes that happen at the scale of single particles to the overall brightness of the aurora.

Taken together, these findings show that the low-altitude auroral region is not only a place where incoming wave energy is used up. It is also an active source of Alfvén waves. This fundamentally changes the standard view of how energy moves through the magnetosphere at Jupiter, and possibly in other places with strongly magnetized plasma.
